title: SYSK Selects: Is lethal injection humane?
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of the 2013 episode on how lethal injection works. Hosts Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant walk through the history of the death penalty in the US (the 1972 Furman v. Georgia ruling, the 1976 Gregg v. Georgia reinstatement, and the origins of lethal injection in Oklahoma/Texas-era reform), the stages of an execution from death row and death watch through last meals, witnesses, and the IV setup, and the drug protocols (the three-drug cocktail of anesthetic, paralytic, and potassium chloride; the shift to single-drug pentobarbital and the propofol and compounding pharmacy shortages). They cover medical ethics, difficulty finding veins, botched executions, alternatives such as firing squad, electrocution, and nitrogen inert gas asphyxiation, and racial disparities in capital cases. The episode closes with a listener mail segment from Whitney in Provo, Utah, and the sign-off.

segments.title: Selects intro and holiday framing
segments.summary: Josh introduces this SYSK Selects rerun of the lethal injection episode, originally released around Christmas 2013, and says it is worth knowing what the state does in citizens' names.

segments.title: Recent executions and the origins of lethal injection
segments.summary: The hosts discuss a recent Missouri execution of Joseph Paul Franklin and Larry Flynt's opposition, then the 1972 Furman ruling halting executions, the 1976 Gregg ruling reinstating them, and the reasons lethal injection replaced hanging and electrocution. They note Julius Mount Bleyer's nineteenth-century proposal and that the US was the first country to adopt lethal injection.

segments.title: Death row, death watch, and last meals
segments.summary: The hosts describe death row, the move to death watch, and state variations in last meal policies, including the outrage over an elaborate Oklahoma-style last meal request and the legislative response. They discuss the Lapham's Quarterly article and the historic practice of getting condemned men drunk.

segments.title: Witnesses and the history of public executions
segments.summary: The hosts explain the witness requirements, including silent state-selected and reputable citizen witnesses, and trace the history of public executions to the 1936 Rainey Bethea hanging in Kentucky. They also note Alabama's jury sentencing rules and state variations in viewing arrangements such as Illinois' closed-circuit feed.

segments.title: Final preparations and the execution chamber
segments.summary: The hosts walk through the final hours: showering, dressing, EKG hookup, final statements, restraint on the gurney, and IV line placement, with the anti-room where executioners administer drugs unseen, sometimes with a decoy setup.

segments.title: Drug protocols: three-drug cocktail, pentobarbital, and shortages
segments.summary: The hosts explain the traditional three-drug cocktail of an anesthetic, a paralytic, and potassium chloride, and the reasons paralytics were questioned. They describe the shift to single-drug pentobarbital, the manufacturer's objection, the propofol refusal by its maker and hospitals, and the turn to compounding pharmacies and midazolam amid shortages.

segments.title: Medical ethics, vein access, and alternative methods
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the American Medical Association's attempt to revoke licenses of doctors involved in executions, difficulty finding veins in former drug users, and the risk of pain from improper drug delivery. They describe nitrogen inert gas asphyxiation as a possibly more humane alternative and compare firing squads, guillotines and the reliability of execution methods.

segments.title: Racial disparities in capital cases
segments.summary: The hosts note racial disparities in death penalty cases, including that most victims in recent capital cases have been white.

segments.title: Listener mail from Whitney in Provo, Utah
segments.summary: Whitney, a band teacher from Provo, Utah, writes that the show helped her through a stressful year with a new job, a move, and a new baby, and says her daughter has listened since infancy.

segments.title: Sign-off and social media
segments.summary: The hosts invite listeners to share stories through Twitter, Facebook, email, and the website, and sign off.
